title: Database Transactions in Applications
learning_outcomes: Describe the purpose and main terms of Database Transactions in Applications.
Use or interpret an appropriate PostgreSQL example connected to transaction boundaries.
Identify one edge case and select a safe way to verify the expected result.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on Database Transactions in Applications. Its primary job is to help you connect applications through parameterized drivers and transaction-safe workflows, with migrations tied to releases. The listed PDF subtopics define the coverage expected here; work through them in order and connect each one to an example, edge case and checkable result.
content.why_it_matters: This topic matters because PostgreSQL systems must preserve correct results as data grows and more sessions or services interact with it. Practicing database transactions in applications teaches you to make assumptions explicit, apply the right SQL or operational tool, and verify behavior instead of relying on a demonstration that only worked once.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Keep the problem small: connect applications through parameterized drivers and transaction-safe workflows, with migrations tied to releases. A PostgreSQL feature should be chosen for the semantics it provides, not just because it is available. Before executing a change, state the inputs, expected output and boundary conditions. The example below is intentionally small enough to inspect; it illustrates the idea but is not a substitute for a test against your schema and PostgreSQL version.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Database Transactions in Applications
content_blocks.expected_output: Both SELECTs return their values; the savepoint demonstrates returning to an earlier transaction point. No data is modified.
content_blocks.safety_note: The example is non-mutating, but the same control flow applies to data-changing statements.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Execute the block in a scratch session that supports explicit transactions.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For a read-only SELECT or inspection command, no reset is needed. For DDL/DML, use a disposable database; capture the starting state, run the example, inspect the result, and ROLLBACK or drop the lab objects as appropriate. Do not use production data or credentials.

task: Create a short practice artifact for “Database Transactions in Applications”: explain its goal, show one example linked to “Transaction boundaries”, state the expected result, and include one edge/failure case and verification method. Use a disposable database or static artifact as appropriate.
hints: Start with the listed subtopics, especially “Transaction boundaries”, and describe the expected behavior in your own words.
Run or inspect the smallest example that demonstrates the behavior; do not add unrelated features before it is verified.
When the result surprises you, capture the exact SQL/error, check version and permissions, and change one assumption at a time.
expected_output: A reviewable note or query for Database Transactions in Applications, with an explanation of “Transaction boundaries”, expected behavior, and a documented edge-case check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying the example without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Object names, data types, privileges, extensions and data distribution affect database behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: List schema/version assumptions and test with a tiny synthetic dataset first.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a single successful query as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: A happy-path result does not test invalid input, concurrent sessions, permissions, recovery or query performance.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one negative/edge case and record the evidence that confirms the expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Making a production change directly from a lesson.
common_mistakes.why: DDL, data updates, role changes and operational commands can affect data or availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use an isolated lab, reviewed migration, least privilege, rollback/recovery plan and a second-person review for production.

summary: Database Transactions in Applications fits into the broader goal to connect applications through parameterized drivers and transaction-safe workflows, with migrations tied to releases.
Use the curriculum subtopics as a completeness checklist: Transaction boundaries, Committing and rolling back, Maintaining consistency across related writes.
State the schema/version assumptions and verify one normal case plus an edge case before trusting the result.
